text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/05/29 - Essay - 01
Buildings and streets form a city neighborhood.
Pexels · 21576133
Getting to know a city
To explore a neighbourhood is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared
experience. The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports preparation while
withholding the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: walking slowly helps us notice details we usually miss. Here, we stop to look at a doorway instead of hurrying to
the next landmark. The arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract ideal of order.
Its success is consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification begins to
unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since respecting local routines makes a visit more considerate. In
concrete terms, we keep an entrance clear while taking a photograph of the street. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience supplies
the standard against which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer. Attentiveness to
others makes that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Write about an attempt to explore a neighbourhood that did not go as planned. Explain two lessons, each supported by a specific incident. Use four short
paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss walking slowly helps us
notice details we usually miss with an example; discuss respecting local routines makes a visit more considerate with a different example; conclude by
connecting the two points.)
